question: What are the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming?

options.text: Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism
Classes, Objects, Methods, Variables
Interfaces, Abstract classes, Enums, Records
Compilation, Interpretation, Execution, Garbage Collection

explanation: The four OOP pillars: Encapsulation (bundling data + behavior, hiding internals), Inheritance (subclasses inherit from superclasses), Polymorphism (same interface, different behavior), Abstraction (hiding complexity, exposing only what's needed). These principles enable maintainable, reusable, and modular code.

question: What is the difference between `==` and `.equals()` in Java?

options.text: They are identical — both compare object content
`==` compares object references (memory addresses); `.equals()` compares object content (unless overridden)
`.equals()` compares references; `==` compares content
`==` works for primitives only; `.equals()` works for objects only

explanation: `==` checks if two references point to the same object in memory. `.equals()` checks logical equality — its default implementation (from Object) is also reference equality, but classes like String, Integer, and List override it to compare content. Always use `.equals()` for object comparison.

question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?

options.text: Abstract classes can have constructors and state; interfaces (pre-Java 8) could only have abstract methods — now interfaces can have default and static methods but cannot have instance state
Interfaces can be instantiated; abstract classes cannot
Abstract classes support multiple inheritance; interfaces do not
There is no difference — they are interchangeable

explanation: Abstract class: can have constructors, instance fields, concrete methods, and abstract methods. A class can extend only one abstract class. Interface: no instance fields (only static final constants), all methods implicitly public. Since Java 8, interfaces can have `default` and `static` methods; since Java 9, `private` methods. A class can implement multiple interfaces.

question: What does `final` mean when applied to a variable, method, and class?

options.text: Variable: immutable value; Method: cannot be overridden; Class: cannot be subclassed
Variable: null by default; Method: runs last; Class: abstract
All three mean the same thing — the element cannot be changed
Variable: thread-safe; Method: synchronized; Class: singleton

explanation: `final` variable: its reference cannot be reassigned (but the object it points to can still be mutated unless the object itself is immutable). `final` method: cannot be overridden in subclasses. `final` class: cannot be extended (e.g., `String`, `Integer`). `static final` fields are compile-time constants by convention.

question: What is method overloading vs method overriding?

options.text: Overloading: same method name, different parameters (compile-time); Overriding: subclass redefines superclass method (runtime)
Overloading: runtime polymorphism; Overriding: compile-time polymorphism
They are the same concept with different names
Overloading is for interfaces; Overriding is for abstract classes

explanation: Overloading (static/compile-time polymorphism): same method name, different parameter types or count in the same class. The compiler decides which to call. Overriding (dynamic/runtime polymorphism): subclass provides its own implementation of a superclass method with the same signature. The JVM decides at runtime based on the actual object type.

question: What is the difference between `String`, `StringBuilder`, and `StringBuffer`?

options.text: String: immutable, thread-safe; StringBuilder: mutable, not thread-safe (fast); StringBuffer: mutable, thread-safe (slower)
They are all immutable — only the syntax differs
StringBuilder is for single characters; StringBuffer is for multiple
String is deprecated; use StringBuilder or StringBuffer instead

explanation: `String` is immutable — every concatenation creates a new object. `StringBuilder` is mutable and not synchronized — use in single-threaded code. `StringBuffer` is mutable and synchronized — use when shared across threads (but slow). In practice, use `StringBuilder` in loops and `String` for simple cases where the compiler already optimizes.

question: What is the Java String pool and how does it affect memory?

options.text: The String pool is a network connection pool for database strings
The String pool is a special heap area where string literals are interned — JVM reuses existing String objects with the same value to save memory
The String pool stores all strings in native memory (off-heap)
The String pool is a fixed-size buffer that causes OutOfMemoryError when full

explanation: String literals (e.g., `"hello"`) are automatically interned in the string pool. `String a = "hello"; String b = "hello"; a == b` is `true` because they reference the same pooled object. `new String("hello")` bypasses the pool, creating a new heap object. `String.intern()` manually adds a string to the pool. Since Java 7, the pool lives in the heap (was PermGen before).

question: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?

options.text: Autoboxing is automatic type casting between numeric types
Autoboxing is the automatic conversion between primitive types (int, double) and their wrapper classes (Integer, Double); unboxing is the reverse
Autoboxing packages an object into a container class for shipping
Autoboxing and unboxing only apply to the String class

explanation: The compiler automatically converts: `int i = 5; Integer boxed = i;` (autoboxing) and `Integer boxed = 10; int i = boxed;` (unboxing). Pitfalls: `Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000; a == b` is `false` (different objects). But `Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b` is `true` — Integer caches -128 to 127. Unboxing a null throws NullPointerException.

question: What is the difference between `static` and instance members?

options.text: Static members belong to the class itself (shared across all instances); instance members belong to each individual object
Static members are thread-safe; instance members are not
Static methods can access instance variables; instance methods cannot access static variables
There is no difference — `static` is just an optimization hint

explanation: Static members (fields, methods, nested classes) belong to the Class object — one copy shared across all instances, accessed via `ClassName.member`. Instance members belong to each object created with `new`. Static methods cannot access `this` or instance fields directly. Static initialization blocks run once when the class is loaded.

question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?

options.text: Checked exceptions must be declared or handled at compile time; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses) do not
Checked exceptions crash the JVM; unchecked exceptions are recoverable
Unchecked exceptions must be caught; checked exceptions are optional
There is no difference — all exceptions behave the same

explanation: Checked exceptions (IOException, SQLException) extend Exception but not RuntimeException. The compiler forces you to either catch them or declare `throws`. Unchecked exceptions (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) extend RuntimeException — no compiler enforcement. Rule of thumb: use checked exceptions for recoverable conditions a caller should handle; use unchecked for programming errors.

question: What is the `this` keyword and what is `super` in Java?

options.text: `this` refers to the current object; `super` refers to the parent class
`this` refers to the class; `super` refers to the interface
Both refer to the current object — `super` just has higher priority
`this` is for methods; `super` is for constructors only

explanation: `this` refers to the current instance — used to disambiguate fields from parameters (`this.name = name`), call another constructor in the same class (`this(...)`), or pass the current object. `super` refers to the parent class — used to call parent constructor (`super(...)`, must be first line), call overridden parent methods (`super.method()`), or access parent fields.

question: What is the `instanceof` operator and what is pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+)?

options.text: instanceof checks if an object is null
instanceof tests if an object is an instance of a type; pattern matching (Java 16+) combines the test and cast into one expression
instanceof is deprecated — use getClass() instead
instanceof only works with interfaces, not classes

explanation: Traditional: `if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; }`. Pattern matching (Java 16+): `if (obj instanceof String s) { }` — combines the check and cast, binding `s` in scope. Returns `false` for `null`. Used in `switch` expressions (Java 21 sealed classes + pattern matching).

question: What are Java records (Java 16+) and what problem do they solve?

options.text: Records are a faster version of regular classes
Records are immutable data carrier classes that auto-generate constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString from declared components
Records are Java's version of database records — they map to database rows
Records are deprecated classes that store legacy data

explanation: `record Point(int x, int y) {}` auto-generates: canonical constructor, `x()` and `y()` accessor methods, `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()`. Records are implicitly `final` and cannot extend other classes. They make simple DTOs, value objects, and tuple-like structures much less verbose than equivalent POJOs.

question: What are sealed classes in Java (Java 17+)?

options.text: Sealed classes are encrypted classes that require a license key
Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend or implement them — enabling exhaustive pattern matching
Sealed classes cannot be instantiated — they are like abstract classes
Sealed classes are final classes renamed for clarity

explanation: `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}` — only the listed classes can implement Shape. Each permitted class must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. Together with pattern matching switch, this enables exhaustive matching (compiler warns if a case is missing), similar to algebraic data types in functional languages.

question: What is the difference between `int` and `Integer` in Java?

options.text: `int` is signed; `Integer` is unsigned
`int` is a primitive — stored directly on the stack; `Integer` is a wrapper object on the heap — can be null, used in collections
`Integer` is faster than `int` because it is pre-cached
They are identical — Java auto-converts them everywhere

explanation: `int` (primitive): 4 bytes, stored on the stack (or in-object if a field), cannot be null, faster. `Integer` (wrapper class): an object on the heap, can be null, required for generics (`List<Integer>` not `List<int>`). Java's autoboxing converts between them automatically but with performance and NullPointerException risks.

question: What is the difference between deep copy and shallow copy?

options.text: Shallow copy: copies primitive fields only; Deep copy: copies all fields including objects
Shallow copy: copies an object and its references (nested objects are shared); Deep copy: recursively copies all nested objects — fully independent
Deep copy uses clone(); Shallow copy uses the copy constructor
They are identical — Java always makes deep copies

explanation: Shallow copy copies the object's fields. For reference fields, the copy and original share the same nested objects — mutating the nested object in one affects the other. Deep copy recursively copies all nested objects — fully independent. Java's `Object.clone()` is shallow by default. Implement deep copy via copy constructors, serialization, or a copying library (MapStruct).

question: What are access modifiers in Java and what do they control?

options.text: public, protected, default, private — control memory allocation
public: accessible everywhere; protected: package + subclasses; default (no modifier): package only; private: class only
public, private, package, friend — control thread access
Access modifiers only apply to methods, not fields or classes

explanation: From most to least restrictive: `private` (same class) → `default`/package-private (same package) → `protected` (same package + subclasses) → `public` (everywhere). Best practice: keep fields `private`, expose via getters/setters (encapsulation). Use the most restrictive modifier that works for your design.

question: What is the contract between `hashCode()` and `equals()` in Java?

options.text: If two objects are equal via equals(), they must have the same hashCode()
hashCode() and equals() are independent — no contract exists
If two objects have the same hashCode(), they must be equal via equals()
hashCode() must always return a unique value for each object

explanation: The contract: (1) If `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must be true. (2) The reverse is NOT required — objects with the same hashCode may not be equal (hash collision). If you override `equals()`, you MUST override `hashCode()`. Breaking this contract causes HashMap/HashSet to lose objects — they'd be stored but never found.

question: What is a functional interface and what is `@FunctionalInterface`?

options.text: A functional interface is any interface in the java.util.function package
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method — the `@FunctionalInterface` annotation enforces this at compile time and enables lambda expressions
A functional interface is one that contains only static methods
A functional interface is deprecated — use abstract classes instead

explanation: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). `@FunctionalInterface` causes a compile error if you accidentally add a second abstract method. Lambda expressions and method references are syntactic sugar for implementing functional interfaces. Built-in examples: `Runnable`, `Callable`, `Comparator`, and the `java.util.function` family.

question: What is covariance and contravariance in Java generics?

options.text: Covariance: `List<Dog>` is a subtype of `List<Animal>` — this is how Java generics work by default
Java generics are invariant by default — `List<Dog>` is NOT a subtype of `List<Animal>`. Covariance uses `? extends T` (read-only); contravariance uses `? super T` (write-oriented)
Covariance and contravariance only apply to arrays, not generics
Covariance uses `? super T`; contravariance uses `? extends T`

explanation: Java generics are invariant: `List<Dog>` is not a `List<Animal>` (unlike arrays which are covariant and type-unsafe). Wildcards add flexibility: `List<? extends Animal>` (covariant, read-only — producer) accepts `List<Dog>` or `List<Cat>`. `List<? super Dog>` (contravariant, write-oriented — consumer) accepts `List<Animal>` or `List<Object>`. Remember: PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

question: What is type erasure in Java generics?

options.text: Type erasure deletes unused type variables from compiled bytecode
At runtime, generic type parameters are erased and replaced with Object (or the upper bound) — generic type information is only available at compile time
Type erasure is a security feature that prevents reflection from reading class types
Type erasure converts Java types to their C++ equivalents

explanation: Java generics are a compile-time feature. The compiler checks types then erases them — `List<String>` becomes `List` in bytecode. Consequences: you cannot do `new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, or create generic arrays `T[]`. At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class. This design maintained backward compatibility with pre-generics Java.

question: What is the try-with-resources statement in Java?

options.text: A try block that automatically retries failed operations
A try block that automatically calls close() on declared resources when the block exits — even if an exception is thrown
A try block that allocates resources from a connection pool
A try block that catches all resource-related exceptions

explanation: Any class implementing `AutoCloseable` (or `Closeable`) can be used in try-with-resources. `close()` is called automatically in the reverse order of declaration, even if an exception occurred — no finally block needed. If both the try body and `close()` throw, the close exception is suppressed (accessible via `getSuppressed()`).

question: What are Java enums and how are they more powerful than constants?

options.text: Enums are just named integer constants — identical to public static final int
Enums are full classes: each constant is an instance, can have fields, constructors, and methods — plus type safety and built-in name/ordinal/values()/valueOf()
Enums cannot have methods — only constant values
Enums are deprecated in favor of sealed classes

explanation: Java enums are full-featured classes. Each constant is a singleton instance. Enums can have fields, constructors, and methods. They support abstract methods (each constant provides its own implementation). Built-in: `values()` (all constants), `valueOf(String)`, `name()`, `ordinal()`. Safe for use in switch expressions. Can implement interfaces.

question: What is the difference between `throw` and `throws` in Java?

options.text: `throw` declares exceptions; `throws` actually throws them
`throw` actually throws an exception instance; `throws` declares in the method signature which checked exceptions may propagate
They are identical — just different syntax for the same operation
`throws` is for runtime exceptions; `throw` is for checked exceptions

explanation: `throw new IllegalArgumentException("msg")` — the statement that actually throws an exception at that point. `throws IOException` in a method signature — declares that the method may throw this checked exception, forcing callers to handle or propagate it. `throws` is part of the method contract; `throw` is the execution action.

question: What are Java's primitive types and their sizes?

options.text: byte(8), short(16), int(32), long(64), float(32), double(64), char(16), boolean(1)
byte(4), short(8), int(16), long(32), float(64), double(128), char(8), boolean(8)
All primitives are 32-bit — size depends on JVM implementation
Java has no primitive types — everything is an object

explanation: 8 primitives: `byte` (8-bit, -128 to 127), `short` (16-bit), `int` (32-bit, most common integer), `long` (64-bit, suffix `L`), `float` (32-bit IEEE 754, suffix `f`), `double` (64-bit IEEE 754, default for decimals), `char` (16-bit Unicode, 0–65535), `boolean` (true/false, JVM-dependent size but logically 1 bit). Primitives are stored by value, not reference.

question: What is the difference between a constructor and a method in Java?

options.text: A constructor initializes a new object and has the same name as its class; a method defines behavior and has a return type
A constructor must be static; a method must be final
Constructors are inherited by subclasses; methods are not
A constructor can be called only after an object has been created

explanation: A constructor initializes an instance when it is created. It has the same name as the class and declares no return type, not even void. Methods represent behavior, have a declared return type (or void), and can be called after object creation. Constructors are not inherited, although a subclass constructor can invoke a superclass constructor using super().

question: Why is String immutable in Java, and what are the practical benefits?

options.text: Immutability prevents strings from being garbage collected
Immutability supports safe sharing, string-pool reuse, stable hash codes, and safer use in security-sensitive APIs
Immutability means String objects are stored only on the stack
String is immutable only when declared with final

explanation: A String's value cannot change after construction. Immutability makes strings safe to share across threads, enables reuse through the string pool, keeps hash codes stable for map keys, and reduces risks when strings represent paths, class names, or other security-sensitive values. Declaring a String reference final prevents reassignment of that reference; it is not what makes String immutable.

question: What is the difference between `==` and `equals()` when comparing Java objects?

options.text: `==` compares object state; `equals()` compares memory addresses
`==` compares references for objects; `equals()` compares logical equality when the class overrides it
`equals()` always compares references, while `==` calls the object's hashCode()
They are interchangeable for all Java objects

explanation: For reference types, `==` tests whether two references point to the same object. `equals()` is a method whose default implementation in Object also tests identity, but classes such as String override it to compare logical content. When overriding equals(), also follow the equals/hashCode contract.

question: What is the purpose of `super()` in a Java constructor?

options.text: It creates a new instance of the current class
It invokes a constructor of the direct superclass
It invokes an overridden method in a subclass
It prevents the superclass from being initialized

explanation: A constructor can invoke a superclass constructor with super(...). If no explicit constructor invocation is written, Java inserts a no-argument super() call when applicable. The superclass constructor runs before the subclass constructor body, ensuring inherited state is initialized first.

question: What is the difference between `? extends T` and `? super T` in Java generics?

options.text: `extends` is generally used when reading values as T; `super` is generally used when adding T values
`extends` allows adding any object; `super` allows reading only Object
Both wildcards make a collection immutable
`super` is only valid for interfaces

explanation: The PECS guideline means Producer Extends, Consumer Super. A `? extends T` reference is useful when a structure produces T values; you can safely read values as T, but generally cannot add a T because the actual subtype is unknown (apart from null). A `? super T` reference is useful when consuming T values; you can add T instances, while reads are typed as Object.
